summary: Outpost Days! is a game where students run a lunar or Martian outpost for 10 days. Each day they make one decision (exercise, sleep, repairs, sheltering from a solar storm, etc.) and allocate a power budget across three areas: life support, radiation shielding, and science. However, each choice has a cost, since for example spending power on science means less for the shield. NASA DONKI space-weather records drive the storm days, including their size and intensity. Radiation rates come from measurements like Curiosity's RAD on Mars, and Chang'e-4 on the Moon; and message delays reflect the real time it takes for light to travel. The game makes engineering decisions fun without oversimplifying them; students see when a mission succeeds or fails by balancing power, health, and a safety reserve.
details:
What it does:

Outpost Days! is a game where students run a base on the Moon or Mars for 10 days. Each day, students make one crew decision (exercise, sleep, fixing equipment, hiding from storms, etc.) and also split their power supply between three sectors: life support, radiation shielding, and science experiments. On storm days, NASA space weather records decide how hard the storm hits. Radiation levels use measured numbers from NASA's DONKI, Curiosity rover on Mars, and China's Chang'e-4 on the Moon. Message delays from Earth are based on the speed of light, showing that on Mars, a warning can arrive too late. At the end of each day, the game shows what changed and explains why, plus a short science fact. After 10 days, players get a star rating based on their science points, or a 'what we learned' screen if the crew ran out of air and food.

How it works:

The game is one HTML file with CSS and JavaScript. Every outcome is different: storm days, warning accuracy (90% on the Moon, 60% on Mars), dust storms, and decisions are random. Before ending a day, players see an overview of what their power plan will do, so they learn from their decisions instead of being surprised.

Why it matters:

The game teaches students that a mission depends on balancing many things. Players learn that their shielding decays from radiation all the time, that forecasts can be wrong/delayed, and to keep an energy reserve.

Tools used:

Made with HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript in a single HTML file that runs in any modern browser and works offline after the first load. CSS3 handles all styling, including custom color properties, Grid and Flexbox layouts, and mobile support. JavaScript runs the game logic. Randomization of storm days, warning accuracy, and decision order allows every game to be different. The game is hosted for free on Netlify.

What makes it creative:

The game turns a NASA space weather archive into a short, replayable game. Storm days use DONKI records, scaled to the actual event and named by date. The Moon and Mars play differently because the physics in each setting differ: lunar warnings take 1.3 seconds at 90% accuracy; Martian warnings take 3-22 minutes each way, are only 60% reliable, and cost waiting time. Mars also adds dust storms and lower radiation, based on rover data. The uncertainty in these missions is highlighted: forecasts can fail, warnings can be false, and risky choices can make it possible to lose. A run lasts 10 days and a few minutes, encouraging replay.

What we considered:

The text was written for young players, being simple/understandable. Every meter includes a text label in addition to color, supporting color-blind users. Buttons were sized for mobile compatibility, while also being accessible on the computer version. A 'words to know' glossary defines key terms. The game says that forecasts can fail, and that the simulation values are concise for easy understanding.
